      "title": "Async legacy writes use the request context and will be canceled when the request finishes",
      "body": "DualWriterMode3.Create starts a goroutine to write to legacy storage and derives its context from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause. When the API request handler returns, the request context is canceled, which cancels the async legacy write. The same pattern exists in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163). Since mode 3 is explicitly asynchronous, the legacy operation should use a detached context, for example context.WithoutCancel plus a timeout, or a background context with copied logger/values; otherwise legacy writes may be aborted before completion."

      "title": "Asynchronous legacy writes can execute out of order",
      "body": "Each mutating operation spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy write with no sequencing, completion tracking, retry, or backpressure. A client can issue update or delete immediately after create; the legacy update/delete may execute before the legacy create, fail, or a delayed legacy create may recreate an object after a delete. This makes the legacy store inconsistent and can resurrect deleted objects despite mode 3 being intended as a safe dual-write fallback. A per-resource serialized queue or other ordering guarantee is needed."

      "body": "In Update, after Storage.Update succeeds, the goroutine calls Legacy.Update with the original rest.UpdatedObjectInfo. Legacy.Update will retrieve the legacy object's current state and invoke objInfo.UpdatedObject against that state. For patch-style updates, or if the legacy store is behind, this can produce a different result than the unified update or fail. The previous implementation wrapped the object returned by the unified update so legacy received the exact final object. Passing the original objInfo risks inconsistent legacy data and unsafe use of request-scoped update info after the request completes."

If an object exists only in legacy storage because of earlier async failure, mode transition, or legacy-only residue, deleting it through the API will leave the legacy object behind. The prior behavior still attempted legacy deletion when unified deletion returned NotFound."

Kubernetes storage strategies can mutate objects during create, and the response may be serialized while the legacy goroutine is running. This can cause data races or inconsistent legacy writes. Use runtime.DeepCopyObject, preferably copying the final object that should be written to legacy, before starting the goroutine."

Track outstanding goroutines with a WaitGroup or worker pool and wait for them in Destroy."

      "body": "The added mode 3 integration subtest runs doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes through the k8s API and immediately queries legacy endpoints. findings.title: Async legacy writes use the request context and will be canceled when the request finishes
findings.body: DualWriterMode3.Create starts a goroutine to write to legacy storage and derives its context from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause. When the API request handler returns, the request context is canceled, which cancels the async legacy write. The same pattern exists in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163). Since mode 3 is explicitly asynchronous, the legacy operation should use a detached context, for example context.WithoutCancel plus a timeout, or a background context with copied logger/values; otherwise legacy writes may be aborted before completion.

findings.title: Asynchronous legacy writes can execute out of order
findings.body: Each mutating operation spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy write with no sequencing, completion tracking, retry, or backpressure. A client can issue update or delete immediately after create; the legacy update/delete may execute before the legacy create, fail, or a delayed legacy create may recreate an object after a delete. This makes the legacy store inconsistent and can resurrect deleted objects despite mode 3 being intended as a safe dual-write fallback. A per-resource serialized queue or other ordering guarantee is needed.

findings.title: Legacy update re-evaluates the update instead of writing the unified storage result
findings.body: In Update, after Storage.Update succeeds, the goroutine calls Legacy.Update with the original rest.UpdatedObjectInfo. Legacy.Update will retrieve the legacy object's current state and invoke objInfo.UpdatedObject against that state. For patch-style updates, or if the legacy store is behind, this can produce a different result than the unified update or fail. The previous implementation wrapped the object returned by the unified update so legacy received the exact final object. Passing the original objInfo risks inconsistent legacy data and unsafe use of request-scoped update info after the request completes.

findings.title: Legacy object is not deleted when unified delete returns NotFound
findings.body: Mode3.Delete returns immediately if Storage.Delete returns any error, including NotFound, so it never attempts Legacy.Delete. If an object exists only in legacy storage because of earlier async failure, mode transition, or legacy-only residue, deleting it through the API will leave the legacy object behind. The prior behavior still attempted legacy deletion when unified deletion returned NotFound.

findings.title: Async legacy create uses the original object without a deep copy
findings.body: The Create goroutine passes the same runtime.Object to Legacy.Create that was passed to Storage.Create and may be the same object returned to the caller. Kubernetes storage strategies can mutate objects during create, and the response may be serialized while the legacy goroutine is running. This can cause data races or inconsistent legacy writes. Use runtime.DeepCopyObject, preferably copying the final object that should be written to legacy, before starting the goroutine.

findings.title: Several duration metrics are recorded with the wrong store
findings.body: Several metric calls record the wrong backend. In Create, a Storage.Create failure calls recordLegacyDuration at line 45. In Update, a Storage.Update failure calls recordLegacyDuration at line 129. In DeleteCollection, the async Legacy.DeleteCollection result calls recordStorageDuration at line 166. This mislabels storage failures as legacy failures and legacy latency as storage latency, breaking dashboards and alerts.

findings.title: Delete storage duration metric uses object name as kind label
findings.body: In Delete, the successful storage duration is recorded with the object name as the kind label: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). The metric expects the resource kind, not the object name. This creates inconsistent labels and can cause high-cardinality metric series for every deleted object name. Use options.Kind like the other methods.

findings.title: Destroy can run while async legacy writes are still in flight
findings.body: Destroy closes both Storage and Legacy immediately, but Mode 3 methods start detached goroutines that can continue to call Legacy for up to 10 seconds. If shutdown or Destroy happens while those goroutines are running, they may use closed storage, fail, or race. Track outstanding goroutines with a WaitGroup or worker pool and wait for them in Destroy.

findings.title: Mode 3 integration test checks legacy APIs immediately after asynchronous writes
findings.body: The added mode 3 integration subtest runs doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes through the k8s API and immediately queries legacy endpoints. Because mode 3 writes to legacy asynchronously, those immediate legacy reads can race and make the test flaky. The test needs polling or eventual-consistency checks for mode 3, or it should not assert synchronous legacy visibility.

findings.title: Mode3 tests race with asynchronous legacy writes and do not verify them
findings.body: The Mode 3 unit tests invoke mutating methods that start goroutines but do not wait for or assert the legacy calls. In TestMode3_Delete at line 230 and TestMode3_DeleteCollection at line 284, no legacy mock expectation is configured, yet the async goroutine will call Legacy.Delete or Legacy.DeleteCollection; this can panic or produce nondeterministic results. Even where expectations exist, tests do not verify async behavior. Add synchronization and AssertExpectations.

findings.title: Legacy async failures are only counted, not logged
findings.body: Async legacy errors are only passed to metrics. For example, if Legacy.Create fails in the goroutine, there is no log entry; the old synchronous code logged such failures. Silent legacy-write failures make divergence and operational problems hard to detect. Log the error with object kind/name and cause.

findings.title: Delete puts the base logger in context instead of the method-specific logger
findings.body: Delete builds a logger with name, kind, and method values, but then sets the context logger to d.Log instead of that enriched log. Downstream code using klog.FromContext will not see the method-specific fields. Use ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log).
